proofs.proof_tex:
Throughout, \(1\leq\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1<\infty\), as required by the declared parameter spaces.  Write \(V=(Y(0),Y(1))\), and define \(\operatorname{logit}(s)=\log\{s/(1-s)\}\) for \(0<s<1\).

First consider \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal M^{\circ}(P_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\).  Strict positivity in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) implies that all conditional probabilities in this paragraph lie in \((0,1)\).  Put
\[
e_{u,x}=\widetilde P(A=1\mid U=u,X=x),\qquad
b_x=\operatorname{logit}(e_{0,x}),
\]
and
\[
\alpha_x=\operatorname{logit}(e_{1,x})-
          \operatorname{logit}(e_{0,x}).
\]
Because \(u\in\{0,1\}\), these definitions give the binary-logistic coordinate identity
\[
\operatorname{logit}\widetilde P(A=1\mid U=u,X=x)
=b_x+\alpha_xu.                                            \tag{1}
\]
If \(s_{u,x}=\widetilde P(U=u,X=x)>0\), then
\[
\zeta_{1,u,x}=s_{u,x}e_{u,x},
\qquad
\zeta_{0,u,x}=s_{u,x}(1-e_{u,x}).                          \tag{2}
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(s_{0,x}s_{1,x}\) in (2) yields
\[
\frac{\zeta_{1,1,x}\zeta_{0,0,x}}
     {\zeta_{1,0,x}\zeta_{0,1,x}}
=\frac{e_{1,x}(1-e_{0,x})}{e_{0,x}(1-e_{1,x})}
=\exp(\alpha_x).                                           \tag{3}
\]
The two treatment inequalities appearing in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) are therefore equivalent, by positivity of the denominator in (3), to
\[
\Gamma_A^{-1}\leq \exp(\alpha_x)\leq\Gamma_A,
\]
which is in turn equivalent to
\[
|\alpha_x|\leq\log\Gamma_A.                              \tag{4}
\]

The conditional-independence condition in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) makes the conditional marginal risk of \(Y(a)\) independent of the realized value of \(A\).  Thus, with the already declared notation \(\mu_{a,u,x}=\widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid U=u,X=x\}\), set
\[
c_{a,x}=\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{a,0,x}),
\qquad
\delta_{a,x}=\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{a,1,x})-
              \operatorname{logit}(\mu_{a,0,x}).
\]
Again using \(u\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
\operatorname{logit}\widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid U=u,X=x\}
=c_{a,x}+\delta_{a,x}u.                                    \tag{5}
\]
By the definition of \(\eta\),
\[
\eta_{a,1,u,x}=s_{u,x}\mu_{a,u,x},
\qquad
\eta_{a,0,u,x}=s_{u,x}(1-\mu_{a,u,x}).                    \tag{6}
\]
Cancellation of \(s_{0,x}s_{1,x}>0\) in (6) gives
\[
\frac{\eta_{a,1,1,x}\eta_{a,0,0,x}}
     {\eta_{a,1,0,x}\eta_{a,0,1,x}}
=\frac{\mu_{a,1,x}(1-\mu_{a,0,x})}
       {\mu_{a,0,x}(1-\mu_{a,1,x})}
=\exp(\delta_{a,x}).                                      \tag{7}
\]
The two outcome inequalities in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) are consequently equivalent to
\[
|\delta_{a,x}|\leq\log\Gamma_a.                          \tag{8}
\]

Conversely, suppose a strictly positive full-data law satisfies the observed-margin, consistency, and conditional-independence conditions of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\), and admits the binary-logistic representations (1) and (5) with (4) and (8).  Reversing (3) and (7) shows that its \(\zeta\)- and \(\eta\)-cells satisfy all four weak cross-product inequalities in that definition.  Hence the law belongs to \(\mathcal M^{\circ}\).  The forward and reverse implications prove the asserted union equality.  In these coordinates \(b_x\) and \(c_{a,x}\) are arbitrary real intercepts except that, together with the distribution of \((X,U)\) and the positive conditional coupling of \(V\), they must satisfy the observed-margin equations.  Thus the assertion is an internal reparameterization of the maintained class, not an identification of that class with any historically defined model.

It remains to establish the closure assertion.  Let \(C\subseteq\Delta_{\mathrm{full}}\) be the set of nonnegative full-data tables satisfying the observed-margin, consistency, and conditional-independence conditions in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\), interpreted on probability tables, together with its displayed weak inequalities in \(\zeta\) and \(\eta\).  More explicitly, the consistency and observed-margin requirements say that the pushforward under
\[
(x,a,u,y_0,y_1)\longmapsto(x,a,ay_1+(1-a)y_0)
\]
equals \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and the conditional-independence requirement is expressed without division by
\[
\widetilde P(v,a,u,x)\widetilde P(u,x)
=\widetilde P(v,u,x)\widetilde P(a,u,x)                   \tag{9}
\]
for every \(v\in\{0,1\}^2\), \(a,u\in\{0,1\}\), and \(x\in\mathcal X\).  The pushforward restrictions are linear equalities in the full-table cells, (9) is a finite collection of polynomial equalities, and each restriction in \(\zeta\) and \(\eta\) is a weak polynomial inequality.  Therefore \(C\) is closed in the finite-dimensional simplex.  Since every law in \(\mathcal M^{\circ}\) satisfies these restrictions, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) gives
\[
\mathcal M=\operatorname{cl}_{\Delta_{\mathrm{full}}}
             \mathcal M^{\circ}\subseteq C.              \tag{10}
\]

For the reverse inclusion, fix \(\widetilde P\in C\).  We construct strictly positive laws in the maintained class that converge cellwise to \(\widetilde P\).  Fix a stratum \(x\).  The declared observed law has \(\lambda_x>0\), \(0<p_x<1\), and \(0<r_{a,x}<1\).  Define
\[
w_{a,x}=\widetilde P(U=1\mid A=a,X=x).
\]
The treatment cells can then be written as
\[
\begin{aligned}
\zeta_{1,1,x}&=\lambda_xp_xw_{1,x},
&\zeta_{1,0,x}&=\lambda_xp_x(1-w_{1,x}),\\
\zeta_{0,1,x}&=\lambda_x(1-p_x)w_{0,x},
&\zeta_{0,0,x}&=\lambda_x(1-p_x)(1-w_{0,x}).
\end{aligned}                                               \tag{11}
\]
Cancelling \(\lambda_x^2p_x(1-p_x)>0\) in the two treatment inequalities gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{1,x}(1-w_{0,x})
&\leq\Gamma_Aw_{0,x}(1-w_{1,x}),\\
w_{0,x}(1-w_{1,x})
&\leq\Gamma_Aw_{1,x}(1-w_{0,x}).
\end{aligned}                                               \tag{12}
\]
Because \(\Gamma_A<\infty\), (12) implies the following exhaustive alternative:
\[
0<w_{0,x},w_{1,x}<1,
\qquad (w_{0,x},w_{1,x})=(0,0),
\qquad\text{or}\qquad(w_{0,x},w_{1,x})=(1,1).             \tag{13}
\]
Indeed, substituting \(w_{0,x}=0\) into the first inequality forces \(w_{1,x}=0\), and substituting \(w_{1,x}=0\) into the second forces \(w_{0,x}=0\); substituting \(w_{0,x}=1\) into the second forces \(w_{1,x}=1\), and substituting \(w_{1,x}=1\) into the first forces \(w_{0,x}=1\).

Consider first the interior case in (13).  Both values of \(U\) then have positive probability given \(X=x\), and every \((A,U)\)-cell is positive.  Equation (9) implies that there is a common conditional probability table
\[
g_{u,x}(y_0,y_1)
=\widetilde P\{V=(y_0,y_1)\mid U=u,X=x\}
\]
which is also the conditional table given \((A=a,U=u,X=x)\), for either \(a\).  Let
\[
\mu_{a,u,x}=\sum_{y_0,y_1}y_a g_{u,x}(y_0,y_1).
\]
Consistency, the observed margin, and the common conditional table imply
\[
r_{a,x}=(1-w_{a,x})\mu_{a,0,x}+w_{a,x}\mu_{a,1,x}.        \tag{14}
\]
Writing \(\rho_{u,x}=\widetilde P(U=u\mid X=x)>0\), the outcome cells satisfy
\[
\eta_{a,1,u,x}=\lambda_x\rho_{u,x}\mu_{a,u,x},
\qquad
\eta_{a,0,u,x}=\lambda_x\rho_{u,x}(1-\mu_{a,u,x}).       \tag{15}
\]
After cancelling \(\lambda_x^2\rho_{0,x}\rho_{1,x}>0\), the two outcome inequalities become
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{a,1,x}(1-\mu_{a,0,x})
&\leq\Gamma_a\mu_{a,0,x}(1-\mu_{a,1,x}),\\
\mu_{a,0,x}(1-\mu_{a,1,x})
&\leq\Gamma_a\mu_{a,1,x}(1-\mu_{a,0,x}).
\end{aligned}                                               \tag{16}
\]
These inequalities and (14) imply
\[
0<\mu_{a,0,x},\mu_{a,1,x}<1.                              \tag{17}
\]
For example, if either risk in (16) is zero, the appropriate one of the two inequalities forces the other to be zero, contradicting \(r_{a,x}>0\) in (14); if either risk is one, the other inequality forces both to be one, contradicting \(r_{a,x}<1\).

Let \(h_{u,x}\) be the product-Bernoulli table with the same two marginals as \(g_{u,x}\):
\[
h_{u,x}(y_0,y_1)
=\prod_{a=0}^1
 \mu_{a,u,x}^{,y_a}(1-\mu_{a,u,x})^{1-y_a}.              \tag{18}
\]
By (17), every cell of \(h_{u,x}\) is positive.  For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), put
\[
g_{u,x}^{(\varepsilon)}
=(1-\varepsilon)g_{u,x}+\varepsilon h_{u,x}.              \tag{19}
\]
This table is strictly positive and has exactly the same two Bernoulli marginals as \(g_{u,x}\).  Keeping the \((A,U,X)\)-table fixed and using \(g_{u,x}^{(\varepsilon)}\) as the conditional law of \(V\) for both treatment values therefore preserves (9), (11), (14), and (15).  It consequently preserves the observed law and every odds inequality, while making every full-data cell in this stratum positive.

Now consider a constant-confounder case in (13), and write its constant value as \(c\in\{0,1\}\).  Since both treatment arms have positive probability and (9) holds, there is a common table
\[
g_{c,x}(y_0,y_1)
=\widetilde P\{V=(y_0,y_1)\mid U=c,X=x\},
\]
whose two Bernoulli marginals are \(r_{0,x}\) and \(r_{1,x}\), by consistency and the observed-margin equations.  Let
\[
h_x(y_0,y_1)
=\prod_{a=0}^1 r_{a,x}^{,y_a}(1-r_{a,x})^{1-y_a}.         \tag{20}
\]
Every cell of \(h_x\) is positive.  For \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), replace the conditional distribution of \(U\) in both treatment arms by
\[
\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}(U=c\mid A=a,X=x)=1-\varepsilon,
\qquad
\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}(U=1-c\mid A=a,X=x)=\varepsilon, \tag{21}
\]
and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal L_{\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}}(V\mid U=c,X=x)
&=(1-\varepsilon)g_{c,x}+\varepsilon h_x,\\
\mathcal L_{\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}}(V\mid U=1-c,X=x)
&=h_x,
\end{aligned}                                               \tag{22}
\]
using each conditional law in (22) for both values of \(A\).  Equations (20)--(22) make every full-data cell positive and enforce \(V\perp A\mid(X,U)\).  Both tables in (22) have arm-\(a\) marginal risk \(r_{a,x}\), so the observed risk remains exactly \(r_{a,x}\).  Equation (21) makes the treatment-confounder odds ratio equal to one, and equality of the arm-\(a\) risks across the two values of \(U\) makes each outcome-confounder odds ratio equal to one.  Since every budget is at least one, all weak odds inequalities hold.  Finally, (21)--(22) converge cellwise to the original constant-\(U\) table as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

Apply (19) in every stratum of the first type in (13), and (21)--(22) in every constant-\(U\) stratum.  The support \(\mathcal X\) is finite, so these stratumwise constructions combine, with the unchanged masses \(\lambda_x\), into a single law \(\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}\).  Every cell of this law is positive; it satisfies the observed-margin, consistency, conditional-independence, and four odds conditions of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\).  Hence
\[
\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}
\in\mathcal M^{\circ}(P_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1),
\qquad
\widetilde P^{(\varepsilon)}\longrightarrow\widetilde P
\quad\text{cellwise}.                                    \tag{23}
\]
Thus \(C\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\Delta_{\mathrm{full}}}\mathcal M^{\circ}=\mathcal M\).  Combining this inclusion with (10) proves the asserted closed probability-table characterization.  The argument uses only joint-cell equalities and weak inequalities on the boundary; in particular, it never evaluates a conditional odds ratio at a null cell.

Fix a stratum \(x\) and suppress its subscript.  Thus \(p,r_0,r_1\in(0,1)\), and the three budgets are finite rational numbers at least one.  The proof uses exact semialgebraic graphing for the mixture roots, stratified first-order optimization, resultant elimination on zero-dimensional strata, and sign-invariant cylindrical decomposition on exceptional strata.

For an arm \(a\), an endpoint \(\vartheta\in\{\Gamma_a^{-1},\Gamma_a\}\), and a new variable \(z_a\), put
\[
 F_a(w_a,z_a;\vartheta)
 =(1-w_a)(\vartheta-1)z_a^2
 +\{1+(w_a-r_a)(\vartheta-1)\}z_a-r_a
\]
and
\[
 d_a=1+(\vartheta-1)z_a.
\]
By Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\), the conditions
\[
 F_a=0,\qquad 0<z_a<1,\qquad d_a>0                                      \tag{1}
\]
select exactly one point, namely \(z_a=\kappa(r_a,w_a,\vartheta)\).  Hence adjoining \(z_a\) subject to (1) is an exact semialgebraic graph construction and introduces neither a missing branch nor a spurious quadratic root.  To record simplicity of this legal root, define
\[
 G_a(z)=(1-w_a)z+w_a\frac{\vartheta z}{1+(\vartheta-1)z}-r_a.
\]
Since \(F_a=d_aG_a\), evaluation on the graph (1) gives
\[
 \frac{\partial F_a}{\partial z_a}
 =d_a\left\{(1-w_a)+\frac{w_a\vartheta}{d_a^2}\right\}>0.                \tag{2}
\]
All divisions and implicit differentiations below are therefore legal on the graph.  Moreover,
\[
 m_{a,0}=z_a,
 \qquad
 m_{a,1}=\frac{\vartheta z_a}{d_a},
 \qquad
 q_a=r_a+(\pi-w_a)(m_{a,1}-m_{a,0})                                    \tag{3}
\]
are rational functions with denominators of known positive sign.

We next make the analytic outcome branches explicit.  Because \(p\in(0,1)\),
\[
 \pi-w_1=(1-p)(w_0-w_1),
 \qquad
 \pi-w_0=p(w_1-w_0).                                                     \tag{4}
\]
Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}outcome\text{-}budget\text{-}extrema}\), applied to (3), therefore yields the following complete branch table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 & H^- & H^+\\ \hline
 w_1>w_0 &(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_0)=(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_0)
          &(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_0)=(\Gamma_1^{-1},\Gamma_0^{-1})\\
 w_1<w_0 &(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_0)=(\Gamma_1^{-1},\Gamma_0^{-1})
          &(\vartheta_1,\vartheta_0)=(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_0).
\end{array}                                                              \tag{5}
\]
On \(w_0=w_1\), equation (4) makes both adjustment terms zero, so
\[
 H^-=H^+=r_1-r_0.                                                        \tag{6}
\]
If \(\Gamma_a=1\), the two endpoint choices for that arm in (5) coincide.  Thus (5)--(6), including their equality faces, are a finite and exhaustive list of legal analytic outcome-sign branches.

We now enumerate the exposure boundary.  If \(\Gamma_A>1\), the two nonconstant boundary arcs of \(D_A\) have the rational parametrizations
\[
 \mathcal A_+(t)=\left(t,\frac{\Gamma_A t}{1+(\Gamma_A-1)t}\right),
 \qquad
 \mathcal A_-(t)=\left(t,\frac{t}{\Gamma_A-(\Gamma_A-1)t}\right),
 \qquad 0\leq t\leq1.                                                   \tag{7}
\]
Their denominators are at least one.  The first equality in the definition of \(D_A\) gives \(\mathcal A_+\), the second gives \(\mathcal A_-\), and the two inequalities say that \(w_1\) lies between these two displayed values.  Consequently (7), with their common endpoints \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), exhausts the topological boundary.  At either endpoint, \(\pi=w_a\) for both arms, so (3) gives \(q_a=r_a\) without assigning an odds ratio at a degenerate latent distribution.  These are exactly the constant-\(U\) corners.  If \(\Gamma_A=1\), subtracting the two cross-product inequalities gives both \(w_1-w_0\leq0\) and \(w_0-w_1\leq0\), whence
\[
 D_A=\{(t,t):0\leq t\leq1\}.                                           \tag{8}
\]
Equations (6) and (8) then give directly \(\ell=\upsilon=r_1-r_0\).  Thus \(\mathsf{CERT}\) treats this case without applying a two-dimensional stationary calculation.

For completeness, the objectives being optimized are continuous on all of \(D_A\).  Indeed, if \((w_n,\vartheta_n)\to(w,\vartheta)\) and \(z_n\) is the legal root in (1), every convergent subsequence of \((z_n)\subset[0,1]\) solves the limiting mixture equation.  Its limit cannot be zero or one because \(r_a\in(0,1)\), and Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\) makes the feasible limiting root unique.  Hence the whole sequence converges to \(\kappa(r_a,w,\vartheta)\).  Formula (3), its positive denominator, and the finite minimum or maximum in the definition of \(q_a^-\) and \(q_a^+\) prove the asserted continuity.  Since \(D_A\) is a closed subset of \([0,1]^2\), it is compact, so both extrema exist.

Consider now one strict sign cell from (5).  On its two-dimensional relative interior, write its rational objective as \(\Phi(w_0,w_1,z_0,z_1)\), constrained by \(F_0=F_1=0\).  Equation (2) gives
\[
 \frac{\partial z_a}{\partial w_j}
 =-\frac{\partial F_a/\partial w_j}{\partial F_a/\partial z_a}.
\]
Thus an interior stationary point satisfies, for \(j=0,1\),
\[
 \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial w_j}
 -\sum_{a=0}^1
   \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z_a}
   \frac{\partial F_a/\partial w_j}{\partial F_a/\partial z_a}=0,
 \qquad F_0=F_1=0.                                                       \tag{9}
\]
Multiplication by the products of the positive quantities in (1)--(3) and (2) converts (9) into a polynomial system without changing its legal solutions.  After substitution of either parametrization (7), the identical argument with the derivative in \(t\) gives the tangential stationary polynomial for every one-dimensional arc cell.  Arc endpoints, the sign-equality face (6), and the constant-\(U\) endpoints are already separate cells.  Saturating the stationary ideals by the cleared mixture, arc, and Jacobian denominators removes components on which the rational derivation is undefined; saturating by the strict-cell boundary polynomials removes components already assigned to those lower-dimensional cells.  Because all saturated factors are required to be nonzero on the cell under consideration, this operation removes no legal point from that cell.

Suppose first that a saturated stationary system is zero-dimensional.  Successive bivariate resultants eliminate \(z_0,z_1\) and then one posterior coordinate.  At every elimination, \(\mathsf{CERT}\) splits off the vanishing leading-coefficient and subresultant cases before proceeding, so the elementary implication
\[
 \text{common finite zero}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{resultant zero} \tag{10}
\]
shows that no solution is lost.  Euclidean polynomial division terminates because the degree strictly decreases.  Square-free factorization leaves finitely many real roots.  For a square-free univariate factor, its signed remainder sequence has constant sign variation away from its roots, and at each simple root the variation drops by one; this follows directly from the sign reversal in the Euclidean remainder identity.  The difference of the endpoint variations consequently counts the roots in a rational interval.  Repeated rational bisection therefore produces disjoint rational isolating intervals for every projected root.  Subresultant back-substitution and the legal inequalities (1) lift every interval to all and only the real solutions of the original system.

For a nonsingular lifted solution, rational interval Newton contraction gives a box mapped strictly into itself and hence certifies its unique zero.  If projected roots collide or a lifted isolated solution is singular, the gcd, square-free, subresultant, and Thom-sign data record the collision exactly; the interval Newton test flags rather than deletes it, and exact algebraic sign evaluation against the original equations and inequalities supplies its membership certificate.  If a resultant vanishes identically or the stationary ideal is positive-dimensional, \(\mathsf{CERT}\) invokes its cylindrical-decomposition branch.  To verify termination of that branch, start in one variable with the signed-remainder isolation just proved.  Inductively, for a finite polynomial family in \(d\) variables, project its finitely many coefficients, discriminants, and pairwise resultants to \(d-1\) variables and decompose there.  On a cell where these projection polynomials have fixed nonzero signs, degrees and root multiplicities are fixed, distinct roots cannot cross, and the isolated real roots form finitely many ordered sections separated by sectors; lifting by those sections and sectors makes every original polynomial sign-invariant.  On cells where a projection polynomial is zero, specialization lowers a degree or records an equality and the same finite recursion applies.  The variable number decreases at projection and every polynomial family remains finite, so the recursion terminates.  It retains an entire stationary continuum as an exact algebraic cell.  This also covers every denominator-zero locus and branch collision on its separately declared legal face, while the original uncleared equations and inequalities reject every denominator artifact and every wrong quadratic branch.

It remains to prove exhaustiveness of the optimization list.  Let an optimizer of \(H^-\) or \(H^+\) be given; existence was proved above.  The finite stratification (5)--(8) places it in the relative interior of a cell of dimension zero, one, or two.  In dimension zero it is already listed.  In dimension one, differentiability along the cell forces the tangential equation unless the objective is constant there.  In dimension two, differentiability forces both equations (9).  A nonisolated set of such points is retained by the cylindrical-decomposition branch.  Hence every optimizer, including every singular or positive-dimensional one, is represented by an enumerated algebraic point or cell.

Finally, algebraic objective values at distinct candidates are compared exactly by refining their rational isolating intervals until they are disjoint.  If two values are equal, reduction in their common algebraic coordinate ring certifies equality.  Exact sign evaluation supplies membership certificates for all original constraints.  Performing these finite operations for \(H^-\) and \(H^+\) returns exact real-algebraic representations and rational isolating intervals for \(\ell_x\) and \(\upsilon_x\).  Repeating independently over the finite set \(\mathcal X\) proves the theorem.  All coefficients were specialized fixed rational inputs throughout; no step purports to return a symbolic atlas over varying inputs.

The proof uses first-order semialgebraic elimination to construct the atlas and an explicit compact-set argument to establish monotonicity and continuity.

By Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}complete\text{-}semialgebraic\text{-}certificate}\), each legal posterior pair, endpoint mixture root, outcome-sign branch, stationary condition, and objective comparison has a finite polynomial description after adjoining the legal root variables.  With the budgets now treated as parameters, reciprocal endpoints such as \(\Gamma_a^{-1}\) are handled by adjoining the equation \(\Gamma_a\vartheta_a=1\); this is legal because every budget is at least one.  For a stratum \(x\), let \(\mathsf{Feas}_x(v,s)\) denote the resulting finite disjunction asserting that \(v\) contains legal posterior and root variables and that the corresponding lower objective equals \(s\).  The graph of the lower endpoint is described exactly by
\[
 \operatorname{Graph}(\ell_x)
 =\left\{(\gamma,s):
   \exists v\,\mathsf{Feas}_x(v,s)
   \ \wedge\ 
   \neg\exists(v',s')\,[\mathsf{Feas}_x(v',s')\wedge s'<s]
  \right\},                                                             \tag{11}
\]
where \(\gamma=(\Gamma_A,\Gamma_0,\Gamma_1)\).  Compactness and continuity, proved in the certificate theorem, ensure that (11) neither loses the infimum nor introduces an unattained value.

Apply the finite projection-and-lifting construction from that theorem to (11), with the observed summaries and \(\gamma\) as coefficients.  Projection eliminates all quantified coordinates and partitions the compact box \(\mathcal B\) into finitely many sign-invariant semialgebraic cells over \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\).  On each cell, the legal optimizer strata and their algebraic objective values are fixed.  Adjoining variables \((s_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}\), the graph equations (11), and
\[
 L=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_xs_x,
 \qquad L=0,                                                            \tag{12}
\]
then gives a finite semialgebraic stratification of \(\mathfrak T_0(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\cap\mathcal B\).  The projection family is augmented by branch-boundary polynomials, discriminants, Jacobian minors, and pairwise objective differences.  After identically coincident descriptions are merged, their zero sets are unions of designated lower-dimensional cells.  Thus optimizer ties, legal-root collisions, constant-\(U\) contacts, and stationary continua occur on recorded lower-dimensional strata in the joint parameter--optimizer stratification, rather than being discarded by a generic resultant calculation.

We next establish coordinatewise monotonicity.  Write explicitly, using Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}outcome\text{-}budget\text{-}extrema}\),
\[
 q^-_{a,x}(w;\Gamma_a)
 =\min_{\theta\in[\Gamma_a^{-1},\Gamma_a]}q_{a,x}(w;\theta),
 \qquad
 q^+_{a,x}(w;\Gamma_a)
 =\max_{\theta\in[\Gamma_a^{-1},\Gamma_a]}q_{a,x}(w;\theta).             \tag{13}
\]
If \(\Gamma_1'\geq\Gamma_1\), the first interval in (13) expands, so \(q^-_{1,x}\) cannot increase.  If \(\Gamma_0'\geq\Gamma_0\), the second interval expands, so \(q^+_{0,x}\) cannot decrease.  Hence \(H_x^-=q^-_{1,x}-q^+_{0,x}\) cannot increase under either enlargement.  Likewise, if \(\Gamma_A'\geq\Gamma_A\), each inequality defining \(D_{A,x}(\Gamma_A)\) remains true with \(\Gamma_A'\), and therefore
\[
 D_{A,x}(\Gamma_A)\subseteq D_{A,x}(\Gamma_A').                         \tag{14}
\]
Minimizing a pointwise nonincreasing objective over the enlarged set in (14) proves that every \(\ell_x\), and consequently \(L=\sum_x\lambda_x\ell_x\) with \(\lambda_x>0\), is coordinatewise nonincreasing.

We prove continuity without invoking a hidden regularity assumption.  The sequential argument in the certificate theorem shows that the unique feasible mixture root is jointly continuous in \((w,  heta)\) for \(r\in(0,1)\) and finite positive \(\theta\).  Therefore \(q_{a,x}\) is jointly continuous, and taking a minimum or maximum over the compact interval \([\Gamma_a^{-1},\Gamma_a]\) makes both functions in (13) jointly continuous in the posterior pair and the finite outcome budget.

It remains only to control the moving exposure region.  Put \(c=\log\Gamma_A\).  For \((w_0,w_1)\in(0,1)^2\), set \(t_a=\operatorname{logit}(w_a)\).  The two exposure inequalities are equivalent to
\[
 |t_1-t_0|\leq c.                                                        \tag{15}
\]
If \(c_n\to c\) and a point satisfying (15) is not a constant corner, keep \((t_0+t_1)/2\) fixed and replace \(t_1-t_0\) by
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}(t_1-t_0)\min\{|t_1-t_0|,c_n\}.
\]
The resulting posterior pair lies in \(D_{A,x}(e^{c_n})\) and converges to the original pair.  The two constant corners belong to every exposure region.  Conversely, every convergent sequence of feasible posterior pairs has a feasible limit because the two defining cross-product inequalities are closed.  These two facts prove Hausdorff convergence of \(D_{A,x}(e^{c_n})\) to \(D_{A,x}(e^c)\), including \(c=0\), where the limiting set is the diagonal.

On the compact product of \([0,1]^2\) and any finite budget neighborhood, the lower objective is uniformly continuous.  Given Hausdorff-close feasible sets, evaluate either minimum at a nearest feasible point in the other set; the two resulting inequalities bound the difference of the minima by the uniform-continuity modulus.  Thus every \(\ell_x\), and hence the finite weighted sum \(L\), is continuous.

For rational or real-algebraic summaries and box endpoints, every coefficient used in projection is an effective element of \(K_{\mathrm{in}}\).  Euclidean remainder sequences, algebraic-number sign tests, and the finite projection-and-lifting recursion therefore terminate and return exact quantifier-free sign cells and algebraic optimizer strata.  Signed-remainder isolation gives rational isolating intervals after a zero-dimensional specialization.  A positive-dimensional stratum is instead returned by its exact sign conditions, so no rational interval is asserted where none could isolate the whole stratum.  This is precisely the output contract of \(\mathsf{ATLAS}\), and it is distinct from the fixed-input contract of \(\mathsf{CERT}\).

The proof uses a local analytic implicit expansion followed by a direct asymptotically linear substitution and a one-dimensional root expansion.

The strict observed-cell conditions put \(b_0\) in the relative interior of its finite-dimensional chart, and the assumption \(\gamma_0\in\operatorname{int}\{\mathcal B\cap(1,\infty)^3\}\) permits two-sided local perturbations of every budget coordinate.  Nonzero denominators and strict inactive inequalities persist by continuity.  The unique active branch and its strict objective separation therefore imply, on a sufficiently small neighborhood, that
\[
 F\{z(b,\gamma),b,\gamma\}=0,
 \qquad
 L(b,\gamma)=\phi\{z(b,\gamma),b,\gamma\}.                              \tag{16}
\]

We justify the local solution and its derivative.  Let \(J=F_z(z_0,b_0,\gamma_0)\), which is invertible by hypothesis, and write \(h=(h_b,h_\gamma)\) and \(v=z-z_0\).  Differentiability gives
\[
 F(z_0+v,b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)
 =Jv+F_bh_b+F_\gamma h_\gamma+\rho(v,h),                                \tag{17}
\]
where
\[
 \|\rho(v,h)-\rho(v',h)\|=o(1)\|v-v'\|,
 \qquad
 \rho(0,h)=o(\|h\|)
\]
uniformly as \((v,v',h)\to0\).  For a small fixed neighborhood, the map
\[
 v\longmapsto-J^{-1}\{F_bh_b+F_\gamma h_\gamma+\rho(v,h)\}
\]
has Lipschitz constant less than one and maps a ball of radius \(C\|h\|\) into itself for a sufficiently large fixed \(C\).  Its successive iterates are Cauchy, because their distances decrease geometrically, and their limit is the unique solution of (17) in that ball.  Consequently \(v=O(\|h\|)\), and substitution in (17) yields
\[
 z(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-z_0
 =-J^{-1}F_bh_b-J^{-1}F_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|).                        \tag{18}
\]
This also proves directly the local implicit solution used in (16).

Expanding the second identity in (16) and using (18) gives, equation by equation,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 L(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-L(b_0,\gamma_0)
 &=\phi_z\{z(b_0+h_b,\gamma_0+h_\gamma)-z_0\}
   +\phi_bh_b+\phi_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|)\\
 &=\bigl(\phi_b-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_b\bigr)h_b
   +\bigl(\phi_\gamma-\phi_zF_z^{-1}F_\gamma\bigr)h_\gamma
   +o(\|h\|)\\
 &=\dot L_bh_b+\dot L_\gamma h_\gamma+o(\|h\|),
\end{aligned}                                                            \tag{19}
\]
where all derivatives are evaluated at \((z_0,b_0,\gamma_0)\).  This proves the two derivative formulas rather than assuming them.

The given asymptotically linear representation implies \(\widehat b_n-b_0=O_P(n^{-1/2})\).  Taking \(h_b=\widehat b_n-b_0\) and \(h_\gamma=0\) in (19), and using \(L(b_0,\gamma_0)=0\), gives
\[
 \sqrt n\,L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)
 =\dot L_b\sqrt n(\widehat b_n-b_0)+o_P(1)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ \dot L_bZ.                                       \tag{20}
\]
Since \(Z\sim N(0,\Sigma)\),
\[
 \dot L_bZ\sim N(0,\sigma_L^2),
 \qquad
 \sigma_L^2=\dot L_b\Sigma\dot L_b^{\mathsf T}.                        \tag{21}
\]

For the frontier displacement, define
\[
 \nu_0=\frac{\dot L_\gamma^{\mathsf T}}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|}.
\]
The assumed nonzero gradient gives
\[
 \dot L_\gamma\nu_0=\|\dot L_\gamma\|=:c>0.                          \tag{22}
\]
By continuity of the branch derivative, the function \(t\mapsto L(b,\gamma_0+t\nu_0)\) has derivative at least \(c/2\) for all sufficiently small \((b-b_0,t)\).  Choose a deterministic sequence \(M_n\to\infty\) with \(M_n/\sqrt n\to0\).  Equation (20) implies that, with probability tending to one,
\[
 |L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)|<\frac{cM_n}{4\sqrt n}.
\]
The mean-value inequality and the derivative lower bound then make the values at \(t=-M_n/\sqrt n\) and \(t=M_n/\sqrt n\) have opposite signs.  Continuity and strict monotonicity give a unique root \(t_n\) between them.  Applying the mean-value inequality once more between \(0\) and \(t_n\) gives
\[
 |t_n|\leq\frac{2}{c}|L(\widehat b_n,\gamma_0)|=O_P(n^{-1/2}).           \tag{23}
\]

Use \(h_b=\widehat b_n-b_0\) and \(h_\gamma=t_n\nu_0\) in (19).  Equations (22)--(23) make the remainder \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\), and the root equation becomes
\[
 0=\dot L_b(\widehat b_n-b_0)+\|\dot L_\gamma\|t_n+o_P(n^{-1/2}).       \tag{24}
\]
Multiplying by \(\sqrt n\), solving for \(\sqrt n t_n\), and using the assumed limit of \(\sqrt n(\widehat b_n-b_0)\) yield
\[
 \sqrt n\,t_n
 \ \Longrightarrow\
 -\frac{\dot L_bZ}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|}
 \sim N\!\left(0,
   \frac{\sigma_L^2}{\|\dot L_\gamma\|^2}\right).                    \tag{25}
\]
Equation (19) identifies \(\dot L_\gamma=\nabla_\gamma L(b_0,\gamma_0)\), so the standard-error constant in (25) is \(\sigma_L/\|\nabla_\gamma L\|\).  If \(\sigma_L>0\), consistency of the stated plug-in estimators and continuity of matrix multiplication, the Euclidean norm, and division by the nonzero denominator give the usual pointwise normal confidence interval.  Replacing the active minimizing branch by the active maximizing branch and replacing \(L\) by \(R\) repeats (16)--(25) verbatim, proving the final assertion.

Fix a stratum \(x\in\mathcal X\).  First suppose \(\Gamma_A=1\).  By Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}exposure\text{-}region}\), every \((w_0,w_1)\in D_{A,x}\) satisfies
\[
w_1(1-w_0)\leq w_0(1-w_1)
\quad\text{and}\quad
w_0(1-w_1)\leq w_1(1-w_0).
\]
Thus the two cross-products are equal.  Expanding them gives
\[
w_1-w_0w_1=w_0-w_0w_1,
\]
so \(w_1=w_0\), including at \(w_0,w_1\in\{0,1\}\).  Write their common value as \(w_x\).  The prevalence formula in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}adjusted\text{-}arm\text{-}mean}\) then gives, using \(0<p_x<1\),
\[
\pi_x=p_xw_x+(1-p_x)w_x=w_x=w_{a,x}
\qquad(a\in\{0,1\}).
\]
For any feasible outcome-odds value \(\theta>0\), the same definition therefore yields
\[
q_{a,x}(w_x,w_x;\theta)-r_{a,x}
=(\pi_x-w_{a,x})(m_1-m_0)=0.
\]
Consequently Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}endpoints}\) gives
\[
q^-_{a,x}(w_x,w_x)=q^+_{a,x}(w_x,w_x)=r_{a,x},
\qquad
H^-_x(w_x,w_x)=H^+_x(w_x,w_x)=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}.
\]
The objective is constant on \(D_{A,x}\); hence
\[
\ell_x=\upsilon_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}.
\]
Summing with the observed stratum masses as prescribed by Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}endpoints}\) gives
\[
L=R=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x(r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}).
\]
Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}envelope}\) identifies the causal ATE set over the closed maintained class with \([L,R]\), so this singleton is point identification rather than merely an outer bound.

Now suppose \(\Gamma_0=\Gamma_1=1\), so \(\Gamma_a=1\) for both arms.  Take a law \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal M^{\circ}(P_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_A,1,1)\).  For fixed \((a,x)\), put
\[
c_{u,x}=\widetilde P(U=u,X=x).
\]
Strict positivity in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}positive\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\) implies \(c_{u,x}>0\) and \(0<\mu_{a,u,x}<1\).  By the definitions of \(\eta\) and \(\mu\),
\[
\eta_{a,1,u,x}=c_{u,x}\mu_{a,u,x},
\qquad
\eta_{a,0,u,x}=c_{u,x}(1-\mu_{a,u,x}).
\]
Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}outcome\text{-}odds\text{-}upper}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}outcome\text{-}odds\text{-}lower}\), with \(\Gamma_a=1\), imply the equality
\[
\eta_{a,1,1,x}\eta_{a,0,0,x}
=\eta_{a,1,0,x}\eta_{a,0,1,x}.
\]
Substitution of the preceding factorization and cancellation of the positive factor \(c_{0,x}c_{1,x}\) give
\[
\mu_{a,1,x}(1-\mu_{a,0,x})
=\mu_{a,0,x}(1-\mu_{a,1,x}),
\]
and hence
\[
\mu_{a,1,x}=\mu_{a,0,x}.
\]
To identify their common value, Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}observed\text{-}margin}\) first gives
\(r_{a,x}=\widetilde P(Y=1\mid A=a,X=x)\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) replaces \(Y\) by \(Y(a)\) on the event \(A=a\), and Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}latent\text{-}ignorability}\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{a,x}
&=\widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid A=a,X=x\}\\
&=\sum_{u=0}^1
   \widetilde P\{Y(a)=1\mid A=a,U=u,X=x\}
   \widetilde P(U=u\mid A=a,X=x)\\
&=\sum_{u=0}^1\mu_{a,u,x}\widetilde P(U=u\mid A=a,X=x)
=\mu_{a,0,x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All displayed conditional probabilities exist because the full-data law is strictly positive and \(p_x\in(0,1)\).  We have proved
\[
\mu_{a,0,x}=\mu_{a,1,x}=r_{a,x}.
\]
Equivalently, the interior outcome odds ratio is \(\theta_{a,x}=1\).  This also agrees with Lemma \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\): Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}mixture\text{-}root}\) gives \(\kappa(r_{a,x},w_{a,x},1)=r_{a,x}\), and the transformed risk is again \(r_{a,x}\).  Since the outcome budget now contains only \(\theta=1\), Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}adjusted\text{-}arm\text{-}mean}\) gives for every interior posterior pair
\[
q_{a,x}(w_0,w_1;1)
=r_{a,x}+(\pi_x-w_{a,x})(r_{a,x}-r_{a,x})
=r_{a,x}.
\]
It follows that \(H^-_x=H^+_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}\) on the interior part of \(D_{A,x}\).  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop{:}closed\text{-}chart\text{-}extension}\) supplies continuous extensions of both endpoint objectives to all of the compact region \(D_{A,x}\), including constant-\(U\) corners.  Because a continuous extension agrees with the constant interior value on the closure, the same equality holds throughout \(D_{A,x}\).  Therefore
\[
\ell_x=\upsilon_x=r_{1,x}-r_{0,x},
\qquad
L=R=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x(r_{1,x}-r_{0,x}).
\]
A final application of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}envelope}\) proves that this singleton is the exact ATE identified set over \(\mathcal M(P_{\mathrm{obs}},\Gamma_A,1,1)\).

proposed.statement: If \(\Gamma_A=1\), then \(w_{0,x}=w_{1,x}=\pi_x\) for every \(x\), so \(L=R=\sum_x\lambda_x(r_{1,x}-r_{0,x})\).  If \(\Gamma_0=\Gamma_1=1\), then on the strictly positive chart the two joint-cell equalities force \(\mu_{a,0,x}=\mu_{a,1,x}=r_{a,x}\) for every \((a,x)\); continuity of the endpoint objectives gives the same point-identification formula on the closed class.
proposed.justification: These reductions are mandatory checks that either absent treatment-confounder association or absent outcome-confounder association removes bias.
proposed.gap: The reductions are implicit in fixed-parameter analyses but have not been stated as boundary faces of a sharp bounded envelope.
proposed.consumer: They provide unit tests for implementations and an interpretable origin for the tipping atlas.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Add the direct class, causal, outcome-odds, mixture-root, and adjusted-mean dependencies used by the proof; the mathematical claim is unchanged.

proofs.proof_tex:
Let \(n\mapsto(\Gamma_{A,n},\Gamma_{0,n},\Gamma_{1,n})\) be any sequence in \([1,\infty)^3\) for which each coordinate tends to infinity, and write \(L_n,R_n\) for the endpoint functionals in \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}endpoints}\) at these budgets.  We prove convergence of both endpoints.

First, there is a budget-free outer bound.  Fix a stratum \(x\).  For any strictly positive compatible law, define
\[
s_{1,x}=\widetilde E\{Y(1)\mid A=0,X=x\},
\qquad
s_{0,x}=\widetilde E\{Y(0)\mid A=1,X=x\}.
\]
Both numbers belong to \([0,1]\) because the potential outcomes are binary.  Observed-law compatibility and consistency give, respectively,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde E\{Y(1)\mid X=x\}
 &=p_x r_{1,x}+(1-p_x)s_{1,x},\\
\widetilde E\{Y(0)\mid X=x\}
 &=(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+p_xs_{0,x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
b_x^-:=p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}-p_x
\ \leq\ 
\widetilde E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x\}
\ \leq\ 
p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+1-p_x=:b_x^+.
\tag{1}
\]
The same inequalities hold for every law in the closed class \(\mathcal M\): by \(\mathrm{def{:}common\text{-}u\text{-}class}\), such a law is a finite-simplex limit of laws in \(\mathcal M^\circ\), and all expectations in (1) are continuous linear functionals of the cell probabilities.  By \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\text{-}common\text{-}u\text{-}envelope}\), \([L_n,R_n]\) is exactly the ATE image of that closed class.  Weighting (1) by \(\lambda_x\) and summing over the finite set \(\mathcal X\) therefore yields
\[
B^-:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x b_x^-
\leq L_n\leq R_n\leq
\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\lambda_x b_x^+=:B^+.
\tag{2}
\]

We next construct common-binary-confounder laws approaching both inequalities in (2).  Put
\[
\varepsilon_n=\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{\Gamma_{A,n}}},
\qquad
w_{1,x}^{(n)}=1-\varepsilon_n,
\qquad
w_{0,x}^{(n)}=\varepsilon_n
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(x\).  These numbers are in \((0,1)\), and direct cross multiplication gives
\[
\frac{w_{1,x}^{(n)}(1-w_{0,x}^{(n)})}
     {w_{0,x}^{(n)}(1-w_{1,x}^{(n)})}
=\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_n}{\varepsilon_n}\right)^2
=\Gamma_{A,n}.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus both inequalities in \(\mathrm{def{:}exposure\text{-}region}\) hold, the first with equality and the second because \(\Gamma_{A,n}^{-1}\leq\Gamma_{A,n}\).  Hence the pair in (3) belongs to \(D_{A,x}\).  Moreover,
\[
\pi_x^{(n)}=p_x(1-\varepsilon_n)+(1-p_x)\varepsilon_n\longrightarrow p_x.
\tag{5}
\]
The joint \((A,U)\)-law determined by \(p_x\) and (3) satisfies, by Bayes' rule,
\[
\widetilde P_n(A=1\mid U=1,X=x)
=\frac{p_xw_{1,x}^{(n)}}{\pi_x^{(n)}}\longrightarrow1,
\qquad
\widetilde P_n(A=1\mid U=0,X=x)
=\frac{p_x(1-w_{1,x}^{(n)})}{1-\pi_x^{(n)}}\longrightarrow0,
\tag{6}
\]
where the limits use \(0<p_x<1\).  Thus this feasible path has precisely the asserted loss of latent positivity.

For clarity, let \(o(t)=t/(1-t)\) for \(t\in(0,1)\).  Given an arm \(a\), a stratum \(x\), and a finite positive value \(\vartheta\), let
\[
m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
=\kappa(r_{a,x},w_{a,x}^{(n)},\vartheta),
\qquad
m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
=\frac{\vartheta m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}
       {1+(\vartheta-1)m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)}.
\tag{7}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}binary\text{-}mixture\text{-}inversion}\), both risks lie in \((0,1)\), uniquely obey
\[
r_{a,x}=(1-w_{a,x}^{(n)})m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)
          +w_{a,x}^{(n)}m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta),
\qquad
o\!\left(m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)\right)
=\vartheta\,o\!\left(m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta)\right),
\tag{8}
\]
and are therefore valid interior-chart risks.

We record the elementary limits from (8).  If \(w_{a,x}^{(n)}\to1\), then
\[
\left|m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)-r_{a,x}\right|
=(1-w_{a,x}^{(n)})
 \left|m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)-m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)\right|
\leq1-w_{a,x}^{(n)}.
\tag{9}
\]
If \(w_{a,x}^{(n)}\to0\), the analogous identity gives
\[
\left|m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}(\vartheta_n)-r_{a,x}\right|
\leq w_{a,x}^{(n)}.
\tag{10}
\]
Because \(r_{a,x}\in(0,1)\), (9)--(10), the continuity of \(o\), and the odds identity in (8) imply the following four limits.  On the lower-endpoint branch \(\vartheta_{a,n}=\Gamma_{a,n}\),
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
m_{1,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n})\to r_{1,x},
&m_{1,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n})\to0,\\
m_{0,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n})\to r_{0,x},
&m_{0,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n})\to1.
\end{array}
\tag{11}
\]
Indeed, for example, the first limit follows from (9), after which
\(o(m_{1,0,x}^{(n)})=o(m_{1,1,x}^{(n)})/\Gamma_{1,n}\to0\); the other arm follows from (10) and
\(o(m_{0,1,x}^{(n)})=\Gamma_{0,n}o(m_{0,0,x}^{(n)})\to\infty\).
On the upper-endpoint branch \(\vartheta_{a,n}=\Gamma_{a,n}^{-1}\), the same argument gives
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
m_{1,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n}^{-1})\to r_{1,x},
&m_{1,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{1,n}^{-1})\to1,\\
m_{0,0,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n}^{-1})\to r_{0,x},
&m_{0,1,x}^{(n)}(\Gamma_{0,n}^{-1})\to0.
\end{array}
\tag{12}
\]

These algebraic candidates are attained by compatible laws, rather than being merely formal values of the objective.  For each \(n\), branch, and stratum, assign
\[
\widetilde P_n(A=a,U=u,X=x)
=\lambda_x\,p_x^a(1-p_x)^{1-a}
  \{w_{a,x}^{(n)}\}^u\{1-w_{a,x}^{(n)}\}^{1-u},
\tag{13}
\]
and, conditionally on \((X=x,U=u)\), take \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) to be independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities given by (7) for their respective arms and the chosen branch.  Make this conditional law independent of \(A\), and set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  Equation (13), interiority of \(p_x,r_{a,x}\), and (7) make every full-data cell strictly positive.  Conditional independence from \(A\) gives \((Y(0),Y(1))\perp A\mid(X,U)\).  Equations (8) and consistency reproduce the observed arm risks, while (4) and the odds identity in (8) verify the treatment and outcome odds budgets.  Hence the constructed law belongs to \(\mathcal M^\circ\).  Finally, the law's adjusted arm mean is exactly the map in \(\mathrm{def{:}adjusted\text{-}arm\text{-}mean}\), because
\[
\widetilde E_n\{Y(a)\mid X=x\}-r_{a,x}
=(\pi_x^{(n)}-w_{a,x}^{(n)})
 \{m_{a,1,x}^{(n)}-m_{a,0,x}^{(n)}\}.
\tag{14}
\]

Combining (5), (11), and (14), the lower-branch stratum contrast converges to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{1,x}+(p_x-1)(r_{1,x}-0)
-\bigl[r_{0,x}+p_x(1-r_{0,x})\bigr]\\
&\hspace{35mm}=p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}-p_x=b_x^-.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
Similarly, (5), (12), and (14) show that the upper-branch contrast converges to
\[
\begin{aligned}
&r_{1,x}+(p_x-1)(r_{1,x}-1)
-\bigl[r_{0,x}+p_x(0-r_{0,x})\bigr]\\
&\hspace{35mm}=p_xr_{1,x}-(1-p_x)r_{0,x}+1-p_x=b_x^+.
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
\]
The lower-branch laws are feasible, so sharpness gives \(L_n\) no larger than their ATEs; the upper-branch laws are feasible, so \(R_n\) is no smaller than their ATEs.  Because \(\mathcal X\) is finite, (15)--(16) may be weighted by \(\lambda_x\) and summed before taking limits.  Together with (2), this yields the two squeezes
\[
B^-\leq L_n\leq \tau(\widetilde P_n^- )\longrightarrow B^-,
\qquad
B^+\geq R_n\geq \tau(\widetilde P_n^+ )\longrightarrow B^+.
\]
Therefore \(L_n\to B^-\) and \(R_n\to B^+\), which is exactly convergence of \([L_n,R_n]\) to the displayed Manski interval.  Equations (3), (6), (11), and (12) also show why the conclusion requires all three budgets to diverge and latent treatment positivity to vanish; no finite-budget recovery or recovery under positivity uniformly bounded away from zero has been proved.
